title: Trump Waives The Graham Act as Washington Floats Russian Gas for Europe
subhead: Trump used Section 115 of his own Russia sanctions law to suspend the threatened 100% tariffs on buyers of Russian energy and set a 60-day review, days after signing a diesel deal with Putin. Separately, US envoys pitched Europe on resuming Russian gas imports as part of a Ukraine settlement — a proposal European officials received with dismay.

sections.heading: The Graham Act Gets a Section 115 Exemption
sections.body:
Trump invoked Section 115 of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act — signed on 18 September — to waive the duties provided for under Sections 112 and 113, suspending for now the threat of tariffs of up to 100% on goods from major buyers of Russian crude and gas, per Indian Express and Mathrubhumi (citing ANI and Hindustan Times). Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the administration wanted a 60-day window to assess the economic consequences, describing India as an important partner and pointing to strain on global energy supply from the Russia-Ukraine war and from shipping and infrastructure disruptions in the Gulf.

The move follows the 9 October Treasury general license authorising the sale, delivery and import of Russian-origin diesel through 7 April 2027, under the diesel arrangement Trump announced with Putin (300,000 tonnes immediately, 500,000 in November, and more after). Reuters and Indian analysts note the waiver has no fixed expiry while Washington retains the power to revive duties. Indian trade expert Ajay Srivastava of the Global Trade Research Initiative told Mathrubhumi the suspension lets Washington keep the tariff as a negotiating chip.

The sequencing matters: the US wrote a secondary-sanctions statute, then carved out an exemption from it within a month, in the same season it agreed to buy Russian refined product. In Washington, Republican Representative Don Bacon told RFE/RL that propping up Russia's war economy is 'terrible,' and Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, a co-author of the law, called the diesel decision an embarrassment that benefits Russia and China.
sections.whyItMatters: The enforcement credibility of the Graham Act is now compromised before a single tariff has been collected. Any future threat to India, China or Turkey over Russian energy purchases will be read against this precedent.

sections.heading: Europe Is Asked to Buy Russian Gas Again — and Balk
sections.body:
US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner told Ukrainian and European officials in Miami this month that a deal to end the war could include resuming Europe's purchases of Russian gas, according to the New York Times, as relayed by Chosun Biz. They reportedly floated the same idea when they met President Zelenskyy in Kyiv a month earlier. The European delegation was, per NYT, very surprised. The pitch also envisions Russian gas moving through Ukrainian pipelines so Kyiv collects transit fees, with European and Ukrainian officials expecting the US to seek a share of the revenue.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov responded that resuming energy cooperation in any form is in Russia's interest and 'may even now be in Europe's own interest.' The White House told NYT it is working on a comprehensive peace plan with economic incentives for both Russia and Ukraine. Separately, the Financial Times reported that Witkoff and Kushner proposed moving some frozen Russian state assets into a separate financial company overseen by the US government.

The context is grim for Brussels: Reuters reported on 12 October that European households and industry face at least another year of high gas prices even if the Iran war is resolved and winter is mild, because storage has been depleted to record lows and must be refilled. European gas is trading near 2022 highs. A Russian supply option is therefore being offered at the moment Europe is most exposed — which is precisely why governments are wary of taking it.
sections.whyItMatters: Gas has been put on the table as a peace-deal currency with Washington taking a cut. If Europe accepts, it reverses four years of diversification policy; if it refuses, it spends another year buying the most expensive LNG in its history.

sections.heading: Hormuz: Record Strike Month as Iran Squeezes the Oman Route
sections.body:
Ship strikes in and around the Strait of Hormuz have already surpassed the entire month of March — the peak of the Iran war — according to maritime data cited by the New York Post. UKMTO counted 12 vessels attacked in the week ending Friday, the highest weekly total since the war began on 28 February: ten in the strait, one in the Persian Gulf, one in the Gulf of Oman. Eight were oil tankers, four container ships; one vessel sank, nine were damaged, three crew injured and two missing. On Saturday the IRGC declared the strait 'closed' and claimed control over the area east of Hormuz, the Arabian Sea and the Gulf of Oman, while a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels caught fire — the IRGC said it hit a mine on an 'unauthorised' route, while US Central Command said vessels were being hit by projectiles and that it had demined the strait. TASS, citing maritime data, put the count from 1-13 October at 22 vessels, with 15 sailors wounded, two missing and one ship sunk.

The operational shift is the targeting of the Oman coast corridor. Most of last week's attacks occurred near Oman rather than Iran — along the alternate route Washington had leaned on. UKMTO also warned it is struggling to report the true number of attacks, since a majority of vessels struck are refusing to report.

Flows reflect the damage. Kpler data cited by FinanceFeeds put oil moving through Hormuz at 11.62 million b/d in the week to 13 October against a baseline of 17.15 million. The IEA's 14 October Oil Market Report was more optimistic on September — Gulf crude exports up 4.4 million b/d to 13.9 million b/d, over 75% of pre-war levels, with total Hormuz flows up 3.7 million b/d to 10.9 million b/d on Gulf of Oman ship-to-ship transfers. The agency explicitly said it left its projections for the rest of the year largely unchanged because of heightened Houthi attacks in October.
sections.whyItMatters: Iran is no longer trying to close the strait so much as to price the workaround out of existence. If the Oman corridor is as dangerous as the strait itself, the market loses its only real bypass.

sections.heading: The Diesel Squeeze Is Now a Political Problem in Washington
sections.body:
The IEA's October report is blunt: global diesel and gasoil availability was cut by 1.7 million b/d year-on-year in Q3 2026 after a 1.5 million b/d hit in Q2, diesel benchmarks remain nearly double the price of crude, and tightness will extend well into 2027. Global diesel exports in September were nearly 700,000 b/d below year-earlier levels. Middle East refined product shipments rose only 210,000 b/d to 1.9 million b/d, against 4.7 million b/d pre-war. The agency expects the diesel crunch to persist even as crude recovers.

The policy response has been improvised. IEA members agreed on 15 October to release more than 20 million barrels of diesel from emergency stocks — less than one day of global diesel demand, per FinanceFeeds — and to accelerate delivery of the remainder of March's record release, estimated at 70-100 million barrels depending on the source. Brent settled at $105.92 on 15 October and traded near $105.21 the next morning; WTI was around $97.40. US crude inventories fell 8.6 million barrels in the week to 9 October, the largest draw since February, while the SPR sits near a record low.

The reason this is now a midterm issue: Trump has publicly blamed Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries for high diesel prices and asked Zelenskyy to stop. Ukraine resumed refinery attacks on 15 October, hitting an installation in the Ryazan region, after Zelenskyy declared a brief truce over and said 'we're done' (Reuters, NPR). Moscow broke with precedent to broadcast images of the strike.
sections.whyItMatters: The US is now managing fuel prices with Russian supply, strategic reserve drawdowns and pressure on Kyiv to stop attacking refineries — three measures that each weaken a different part of its own Russia policy.

sections.heading: India: Relief Without Reversal, and a 31.6% Import Bill Jump
sections.body:
The waiver lands in a market where Indian refiners had already repositioned. India's Russian crude imports fell to around 1.8 million b/d from about 2.7 million b/d in July 2026, per industry executives cited by the Hindustan Times, as buyers added US, West African and South American barrels. Ship-tracking data compiled by National Herald show India averaged about 1.8 million b/d of Russian seaborne crude this year, ahead of China at roughly 1.2 million; India took 1.82 million b/d in September versus China's 1.49 million, and Kpler expects 1.8-1.9 million b/d in October. Urals traded at an average $23 discount to Brent in September.

The cost of that shift is showing in the trade balance. PPAC data cited by Mathrubhumi show India's crude import bill rose 31.6% in September to $15.4 billion from $11.7 billion in August; volumes were up 14.2% to 21.7 million tonnes, and the Indian basket averaged $116.09/bbl versus $90.19. For April-September the bill rose 46.4% to $90.6 billion. The higher bill reflects Hormuz disruption as much as the move away from Russian crude.

New Delhi is still negotiating. Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal has said the first tranche of the India-US trade agreement will be implemented once India secures competitive advantage over peers. Analysts told Mathrubhumi the waiver is relief, not resolution.
sections.whyItMatters: India is paying for geopolitical alignment in hard currency, and the waiver gives it room to buy cheaper crude again without inviting tariffs. Watch whether Indian purchases snap back toward 2 million b/d.

sections.heading: Beijing Reads the Diesel Deal as Transactional
sections.body:
Chinese analysts see the deal as a short-term American fix rather than a sanctions collapse. Cui Hongjian, head of EU studies at Beijing Foreign Studies University, told SCMP that China's approach is to wait and see whether Russia uses the deal as a springboard to loosen the West's entire energy sanctions regime, and that it will have little effect on China-Russia energy trade because Moscow still needs its largest buyer. Zhang Chi of the University of Hong Kong called the arrangement 'self-contradictory' and noted the Graham Act's secondary-tariff mechanism could still be triggered against other importers. Ma Bo of Nanjing University expects the arrangement to be adjusted after the 3 November midterms.

The foreign ministry's Mao Ning kept to the standard line that dialogue is the only way to resolve the crisis. Chinese rare-earth equities offer a separate signal of how Beijing's leverage is priced: the VanEck Rare Earth and Strategic Metals ETF closed Friday at EUR 9.61, just 2.1% above its 52-week low, down 23% year-to-date, with no sector-specific trigger — broad selling tied to inflation and AI-capex worries, per ad-hoc-news. Chinese concentrate pricing was mixed: praseodymium-neodymium oxide up, terbium and dysprosium oxide down, in the China Tungsten Industry News report of 14 October.
sections.whyItMatters: Beijing is treating Washington's Russia policy as reversible, which lowers the incentive to restructure its own buying. That keeps Russian crude flowing east regardless of what the Graham Act says on paper.

sections.heading: Yemen: The Second Export Route Under Fire
sections.body:
The Houthi campaign against Saudi Arabia has moved onto energy infrastructure tied to the Red Sea bypass. On Tuesday, attacks on 'civilian and economic facilities' in Abha, Jazan, Najran and Khamis Mushait wounded 73 people including women and children, per Saudi-led coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, and ignited fires at several oil facilities and utilities, the Energy Ministry said, with operations temporarily suspended (AP). The southern region includes the 400,000 b/d Jazan refinery. The Houthis claimed a strike on Aramco's Dhahran headquarters and threatened Riyadh airport and further oil sites; Reuters reported the vow on 14 October.

This is the part of the war that connects to world markets: as Hormuz is throttled, Saudi Arabia has leaned on the East-West pipeline and Red Sea terminals, feeding Bab el-Mandeb. The IEA noted bypass exports rose 970,000 b/d to 5.6 million b/d in September on the return of East-West flows. That bypass now has its own front line. AP reported that weeks of clashes have added pressure to limited global supplies precisely because the Houthis are targeting the shipping route Saudi Arabia uses while Hormuz is restricted.

Diplomacy is thin. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, meeting Egyptian counterpart Badr Abdelatty on the sidelines of the OIC ministerial in Baghdad on 17 October, said Iran is ready to help halt the Saudi-Houthi confrontations and that 12 years of tension show there is no military solution in Yemen (Trend, citing Iran's foreign ministry). He also said the US halted implementation of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding on cessation of hostilities two weeks after signing it, and that the Hormuz situation is a consequence of US and Israeli strikes on Iran.
sections.whyItMatters: Saudi Arabia's Red Sea outlet was the fallback for Hormuz. With Jazan and southern facilities hit and Taiz under pressure, Riyadh's export flexibility is narrowing at the worst moment for global distillate supply.

bottomLine: Washington spent the week dismantling its own pressure architecture faster than it built it: a diesel deal with Putin on 9 October, a Section 115 waiver of the Graham Act's 100% tariffs on 16-17 October with a 60-day review, and now a proposal to put Russian gas back into Europe as part of a peace settlement. Each step is justified by the same emergency — diesel at nearly double crude, Brent above $105, Hormuz flows at 11.6 million b/d against a 17.15 million baseline, and a strike rate on shipping that has already beaten the war's worst month. The strategic cost is that secondary sanctions are now a threat Washington has publicly declined to use, which is exactly what Beijing and New Delhi are pricing in. Meanwhile the war keeps finding new targets: Iran is pushing attacks onto the Oman corridor, and the Houthis are hitting the Saudi Red Sea facilities that were supposed to replace Hormuz. The next real test is whether European governments accept Russian molecules on American terms — and whether Ukraine keeps striking refineries while Washington buys the fuel they produce.
sources: Indian Express, Mathrubhumi (citing ANI, Hindustan Times, PPAC), National Herald India (ship-tracking data, Kpler), RFE/RL, SCMP (via The Star), Chosun Biz (citing NYT and FT), Reuters, New York Post (UKMTO data), TASS, AP (via HuffPost), FinanceFeeds (Kpler, IEA data), Oil & Gas Journal (IEA Oil Market Report, 14 Oct), Trend.az (Iran MFA), ad-hoc-news (VanEck ETF, China Tungsten Industry News)
